title: The legal profession in 2024: The wider view
author: David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s underlying drivers—corporate cost pressure, technology demand and uncertainty about junior staffing—but does not address workflow unbundling, alternative provider allocation, pricing reform or verification directly enough to establish acceptance of the principal proposition.
qs: This, in turn, is spurring a growing demand for technology that can help these companies produce “more for less” and to more accurately assess the costs and benefits of various investments, including the investment in legal services.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s conditional, non-declinist account: elite-firm compensation and demand remain strong, but their sustainability is uncertain amid client cost pressure, technology adoption and unresolved junior-staffing needs. It reinforces segmentation and adaptation rather than predicting large-firm disappearance.
qs: The question, however, is how sustainable this all is, even for firms that are otherwise doing quite well.
How these larger trends will affect the demand for lawyers and legal services remains unclear.

st.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s core claim that substantial professional change can coexist with persistent underlying structures. He also anticipates continued scrutiny of diversity and inclusion, while withholding a firm forecast about future employment and compensation; the source therefore reinforces continuity and caution rather than independently establishing specific reward inequalities.
qs: And one of the major lessons of that book is that, notwithstanding everything that has changed over this period, there still are some basic structures of the legal profession that have remained remarkably constant.
While the Supreme Court’s recent decision will certainly complicate this inquiry, I do not believe that it will go away.

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core claim that control and influence are shifting toward general counsel by portraying them as central corporate actors who enter decision-making earlier and coordinate cross-functional responses. It does not directly assess whether this authority displaces law firms, produces savings, or varies by jurisdiction.
qs: What has that meant for the general counsels at these organizations?**  **Wilkins:** I’ve been saying now for some time that general counsels are the most important players in the corporate legal ecosystem, and are increasingly important in the world of business, and in all the complex issues that business touches.

Indeed, the more controversial these issues have become, the more lawyers are being brought in at an earlier and earlier stage — working, as I indicated above, alongside professionals in compliance, government and legislative affairs, public relations, and strategy and information systems to develop integrated solutions to these complex problems.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: Wilkins directly supports the cluster’s core case for retaining legal reasoning while broadening lawyer development toward interdisciplinary problem-solving, collaboration and team leadership. He also treats future staffing effects as uncertain and urges educational preparation rather than claiming proven displacement or a settled reform model.
qs: All these changes are pushing law from a “fee for service” model,” in which clients bring lawyers “legal questions,” and lawyers provide “legal answers” which the client then implements, to what I’ve been calling an “integrated solutions model.” In this model, neither the contours of the problem nor the possible array of solutions is strictly “legal” or fully understood by either the client or the lawyer.
Yet, law students are still taught to think and work primarily on their own, with very little attention to preparing students for the complex dynamics of collaboration and leading and managing teams.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Wilkins aligns with the synthesis’s cautious restructuring thesis: technology and other market forces are disrupting legal careers, client cost pressure is driving technology adoption, and junior demand may be especially affected. He does not predict wholesale displacement, instead treating overall lawyer demand as unresolved and emphasizing educational adaptation toward interdisciplinary problem-solving.
qs: How these larger trends will affect the demand for lawyers and legal services remains unclear.
Will we need as many junior lawyers as we have in the past?

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core direction: client cost and risk pressures are increasing demand for technology, potentially reducing junior-lawyer requirements, while complex client problems continue to sustain demand for senior, cross-disciplinary legal judgment. It treats the scale and employment effects as unresolved and does not develop the cluster’s more specific claims about bounded automation, hybrid pricing or alternative providers.
qs: This, in turn, is spurring a growing demand for technology that can help these companies produce “more for less” and to more accurately assess the costs and benefits of various investments, including the investment in legal services.

What skills and dispositions will senior lawyers need to participate in the creation of the kind of integrated solutions at the intersection of law, business, technology, and public policy that their clients will increasingly demand?

kp.k: Legal services are shifting toward integrated multidisciplinary solutions
kp.d: Wilkins argues that technology, competition, globalization and changing client problems are disrupting established careers and moving legal practice beyond supplying legal answers for clients to implement. His integrated-solutions model involves lawyers and other professionals jointly defining problems and possible solutions, rather than treating either as exclusively legal. This is a broader account of professional transformation, not a claim that AI alone causes the shift or a specific prediction about hourly billing.
qs: Well, a lot of those career trajectories are being disrupted, whether by technology, competition, globalization, or by the kinds of problems that lawyers are being asked to solve.
In this model, neither the contours of the problem nor the possible array of solutions is strictly “legal” or fully understood by either the client or the lawyer.

Instead, lawyers work collaboratively with a broad range of professionals to help clients refine their understanding of the problem and the potential array of solutions in ways that promote the client’s ability to continue to make good decisions moving forward.

kp.k: Increasing legalization expands lawyers’ work beyond legal expertise
kp.d: Wilkins describes geopolitical conflict, sustainability, diversity and inclusion, and tensions between shareholder and stakeholder interests as increasingly regulated problems reaching lawyers’ desks. He argues that law is only one component of addressing these matters: clients also need business, technological, political and social considerations incorporated into advice.
qs: These issues are becoming increasingly “legalized”, in the sense that there is more and more law and regulation for clients to navigate.

And yet, law is only a part — and from the client’s perspective, often not the most important part — of navigating these issues which invariably also implicate business, technological, political, and social considerations as well.
Lawyers are increasingly being called upon to be part of multidisciplinary teams providing what I have been calling “integrated solutions” to complex problems that extend far beyond law.

kp.k: General counsels gain earlier, broader strategic involvement
kp.d: Wilkins regards general counsels as the most important actors in the corporate legal ecosystem and says increasingly contentious business-and-society issues bring lawyers into decisions earlier. He describes collaboration with compliance, government affairs, public relations, strategy and information systems. As context for this discussion, he reports a September 2022 Harvard conference attracting over 600 leaders and a subsequent invitation-only session involving 14 general counsels from top companies and their teams; these are convening details, not a quantified study of role changes.
qs: I’ve been saying now for some time that general counsels are the most important players in the corporate legal ecosystem, and are increasingly important in the world of business, and in all the complex issues that business touches.

Following the general session, we held a special invitation-only session for 14 general counsels from top companies and their teams to specifically discuss the role of lawyers in addressing these critical issues, since as you say, these issues are increasingly landing on the general counsel’s desk.

Indeed, the more controversial these issues have become, the more lawyers are being brought in at an earlier and earlier stage — working, as I indicated above, alongside professionals in compliance, government and legislative affairs, public relations, and strategy and information systems to develop integrated solutions to these complex problems.

kp.k: Elite compensation growth faces client cost and technology pressures
kp.d: Wilkins reports rapidly increasing compensation for entering associates and, particularly, lateral partners at the highest-paying firms, widening gaps within the profession. He links upward pressure to strong pandemic-era corporate legal demand and complex new client problems, but questions sustainability as corporate clients seek cost reductions and data-driven risk assessment. The approximately $225,000 first-year salary figure is supplied by the interviewer, not presented as Wilkins’s research finding.
qs: One trend we are seeing for certain is that compensation for both entering associates, and even more for lateral partners, at the very top law firms is skyrocketing, creating a growing gap between the top-of-the-top and even other leading firms, let alone between all these firms and the rest of the profession.
The question, however, is how sustainable this all is, even for firms that are otherwise doing quite well.
Corporate clients are under tremendous pressure to cut costs, and to produce a more data driven approach to risks.

This, in turn, is spurring a growing demand for technology that can help these companies produce “more for less” and to more accurately assess the costs and benefits of various investments, including the investment in legal services.

kp.k: Junior demand and future senior capabilities remain uncertain
kp.d: Wilkins explicitly leaves unresolved whether technology and changing client needs will reduce the number of junior lawyers required. He also asks what skills senior lawyers will need to deliver integrated solutions across law, business, technology and public policy. His recommendation is to prepare students and reconsider professional requirements now, rather than treating workforce displacement as an established finding.
qs: How these larger trends will affect the demand for lawyers and legal services remains unclear.
Will we need as many junior lawyers as we have in the past?

What skills and dispositions will senior lawyers need to participate in the creation of the kind of integrated solutions at the intersection of law, business, technology, and public policy that their clients will increasingly demand?
Only time will tell, but we as a law school and a profession need to start thinking about these issues now if we are going to prepare our students for the careers of the future.

kp.k: Longitudinal career evidence shows mobility alongside persistent inequalities
kp.d: Wilkins draws on The Making of Lawyers’ Careers, based on more than 20 years of data collection around lawyers entering the bar in 2000, to describe persistent professional structures and patterned mobility that can reinforce hierarchies and inequalities. He says early attrition predates current technological changes, with 40% leaving their particular firm within the first three or four years since at least the turn of the millennium. Departure from a firm does not necessarily mean leaving the law-firm sector or legal practice. The interviewer’s one-in-four and nearly 80% turnover figures are separate from Wilkins’s stated evidence.
qs: which is the result of more than 20 years of data collection around the lawyers who entered the bar in 2000.

High rates of early attrition have been a reality for large law firms since at least the turn of the millennium, with 40% of lawyers who join any particular law firm leaving within the first three or four years.
Many young lawyers who leave one law firm join another.

And yet, we also found that while lawyers are likely to move frequently throughout their careers, that these job changes often follow predictable patterns — patterns that often reinforce traditional hierarchies and inequalities within the profession.

kp.k: AI could strengthen small firms and project-based lawyer teams
kp.d: Wilkins predicts that ChatGPT and other technological tools will enable small firms and dispersed teams assembled for particular projects to compete with large firms for sophisticated work. He connects this prospective competitive change to more varied career moves, including transitions into small firms after 15 or 20 years. The interview supplies no measured productivity or market-share evidence for this prediction.
qs: But after 15 or 20 years, many will be working in such settings, just as many of those who start their careers in the private sector will find themselves working in government or elsewhere in the public sector — or not practicing law at all — during their careers.

Indeed, advances in technology make these kinds of moves even more likely, as lawyers learn to leverage ChatGPT and other tools that will make small firms and even dispersed teams of individual lawyers who come together for specific projects able to compete with big firms for sophisticated work.

kp.k: Legal education should prepare adaptable, collaborative problem-solvers
kp.d: Wilkins recommends preparing students for changing careers rather than simply a first job. He preserves the value of traditional legal reasoning but argues that identifying legal problems is insufficient for interdisciplinary challenges such as sustainability, cybersecurity and geopolitical risk. Education should develop problem-solving, collaboration, leadership and team-management capabilities that its predominantly individual approach neglects.
qs: It is imperative that we teach students from the moment they arrive that they are not just preparing to “get a job,” but instead are embarking on careers that will take many different twists and turns.
Traditional legal education is very good at teaching students how to identify problems.
It has paid far less attention to giving students the tools that they need to solve problems.
Yet, law students are still taught to think and work primarily on their own, with very little attention to preparing students for the complex dynamics of collaboration and leading and managing teams.

kp.k: Generational expectations reshape recruitment and organizational accountability
kp.d: Wilkins argues that clients and younger lawyers increasingly scrutinize legal organizations’ diversity, sustainability, wellbeing and public-service practices. He anticipates that millennials and Gen Z will demand meaning and purpose rather than simply security or maximum compensation, putting pressure on employers seeking top talent. His discussion includes an intergenerational wealth transfer estimated by unspecified others at upwards of $50 trillion; these generational claims and projected effects are his interpretation, not demonstrated AI-specific outcomes.
qs: And they’re doing it with the single biggest intergenerational wealth transfer in history, estimated by some to be upwards of $50 trillion.
This is the reason you’re seeing legal employers focusing on issues like meaning and purpose and wellness and sustainability.

If they want to attract the top talent, they must credibly argue that a career in a legal organization provides those things because I think this generation is no longer going to go for either the safe option or even the one that just pays the most money.
And I think they’re going to demand it and that will push change in complicated ways that we can’t predict.

kp.k: Democratic obligations require scrutiny of lawyers’ institutional roles
kp.d: In the election-year discussion, Wilkins frames lawyers as capable of promoting, preserving or undermining democracy and calls for examination of their obligations and accountability. This is a professional-responsibility research agenda within the interview’s wider institutional context, not a claim about AI’s effect on democracy.
qs: What is the role of lawyers in both promoting and preserving democracy, and quite frankly, undermining democracy? And we have seen all of the above.

Given the central — but far from exclusive — role that lawyers play in maintaining the rule of law, it is critical to examine how they understand their obligations to democratic principles and institutions, and conversely, how democracies hold lawyers to account.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wilkins predicts that ChatGPT and other tools will enable small firms and project-based teams to compete with large firms for sophisticated work, making career moves more likely.
pts.d: This is the interview’s most explicit AI-specific prediction. Wilkins also describes corporate cost pressures and demand for data-driven risk assessment as drivers of technology demand, but leaves the consequences for lawyer demand and junior hiring unresolved. More broadly, he identifies technology alongside competition, globalization and changing client problems as forces disrupting legal careers and encouraging multidisciplinary integrated solutions. He does not attribute those broader changes exclusively to AI or predict a specific number of displaced jobs.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The AI-specific competitive prediction is offered as Wilkins’s expert assessment, without a supporting AI benchmark, quantified outcome or deployment case.
pts.d: Wilkins invokes longitudinal research on lawyers’ careers to establish the background of mobility and persistent professional structures. He describes that research as involving more than 20 years of data collection concerning lawyers who entered the bar in 2000. That evidence supports the career context, rather than directly demonstrating that ChatGPT enables small firms to compete for sophisticated work. His discussion of technology demand rests on observations about corporate cost pressures and demand for risk assessment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The competitive prediction is forward-looking from February 2024 and conditional on lawyers learning to use ChatGPT and other tools; no adoption deadline is given.
pts.d: Wilkins places technological change within long-term career development. His reference to lawyers working in small firms after 15 or 20 years concerns career trajectories, not a forecast that AI capabilities will arrive on that schedule. He explicitly treats future demand for lawyers and junior staffing as uncertain. His broader questions about the next 5, 10 or 20 years likewise frame uncertainty rather than specify an AI transition date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include small firms, dispersed lawyer teams, large firms, corporate legal buyers, junior and senior lawyers, and law schools.
pts.d: Small firms and temporary teams are predicted to gain competitive capacity in sophisticated work, while large firms face competition from those providers. Corporate clients seek technology-assisted cost control and assessment of legal spending. Junior lawyer demand is raised as an open question, while senior lawyers face expectations to contribute to multidisciplinary solutions. Law schools are urged to prepare students for changing careers. These latter implications belong to Wilkins’s broader account of technological and market change, not a separately evidenced AI-only forecast.
